project_scope.note: Canonical image anchors now include Clematis and Aquilegia canadensis (two installed, rights-documented columbine photos). Teach shared buttercup-family reproductive structure without pretending opposite Clematis leaves or lack of petals characterizes all Ranunculaceae.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: FIRST inspect a flower: are the many stamens mostly FREE around one to many separate superior carpels? Then identify the showy pieces before naming them petals. Clematis has petal-like SEPALS and no true petals; Aquilegia has both showy sepals AND true spurred PETALS. Finally inspect fruit: clusters of dry achenes in Clematis versus follicles in Aquilegia.
family_diagnostics.floral_parts: Sepals are free and may be petaloid; petals may be present, modified, reduced, or absent.
family_diagnostics.local_clematis: Clematis has opposite divided leaves, no true petals, showy petaloid sepals, many free stamens/pistils, and aggregate achenes with persistent styles.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Common family fruits are aggregates of achenes or follicles.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: The easiest teaching pair is Clematis versus Aquilegia. In Clematis, four showy SEPALS make either an open flower or a leathery urn, and the feathery seedhead consists of ACHENES with persistent styles. In Aquilegia, each of five true petals extends backward into a long spur, and mature fruit is a cluster of FOLLICLES. The family does not share Clematis's opposite climbing leaves universally.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: climbing leaf stalk as Clematis example → sepals not petals → different Clematis sepal arrangements → achene fruit and persistent style → Aquilegia spurred true petals → contrasting columbine habit → free carpels/follicle macro still needed
visual_lesson.intro: Learn the buttercup family with TWO photo-rich genera rather than one: Clematis has showy SEPALS but no true petals, while columbine (Aquilegia) has showy sepals AND backward-pointing spurred true PETALS. The shared family idea is many largely separate stamens and carpels, with fruits often achenes or follicles; leaf arrangement and flower color alone are not family proof.

steps.title: 1 · A Clematis vine climbs with leaf stalks
steps.look_for: Trace the thin CURLING PETIOLE (leaf stalk) as it grasps nearby vegetation. Also look for leaflets attached to a compound leaf. Opposite leaves and winding leaf stalks are Clematis clues, NOT traits that define every buttercup-family plant.
steps.why_it_matters: Starts with a tangible genus example without turning its climbing architecture into a universal Ranunculaceae rule.

steps.title: 2 · The open Clematis flower has SEPALS, not petals
steps.look_for: Count FOUR pale, spreading petal-like SEPALS surrounding many separate STAMENS. This is a MALE old man's beard flower, not the pistil-bearing female flower. The flower has no true petals.
steps.why_it_matters: The key is naming the actual showy part. Not every colorful piece of a flower is a petal.

steps.title: 3 · Sepals can form a leatherflower urn
steps.look_for: Find the NODDING scarlet urn made from four closely arranged, leathery SEPALS. Their tips curl backward. This illustrates how the same floral parts look very different from the open C. drummondii bloom.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates the four-sepal architectural pattern from misleading flower color and petal labels.

steps.title: 4 · A feathery fruit head contains ACHENES
steps.look_for: The silvery feathering consists of persistent hairy STYLES attached to many separate dry one-seeded ACHENES. A single fruit body is not always resolvable in a distant photo, so the dedicated close-up remains pending.
steps.why_it_matters: Clematis has an aggregate fruit made from several carpels, not a single puffball seed or a milkweed-like pod.

steps.title: 5 · Columbine has true SPURRED petals
steps.look_for: Compare five rearward-pointing petal SPURS on the hanging Aquilegia flower with the outer spreading sepals. The spurs are part of TRUE PETALS, unlike Clematis where the showy floral parts are sepals and petals are absent.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the family exception that makes the botanical words SEPAl and PETAl stick—and shows why one genus cannot stand in for the whole family.

steps.title: 6 · Columbine habit looks nothing like a Clematis vine
steps.look_for: Study the columbine's flowering stalks and divided foliage as a second Ranunculaceae growth form. These are two different genera and neither the genus's height nor leaf pairing is a reliable family-only character.
steps.why_it_matters: Recognizing the family requires flowers and fruits, not one habitual growth form.

steps.title: 7 · Examine free carpels and follicle fruit
steps.photo_role: flower center and mature follicles / macro
steps.look_for: In a future close-up, distinguish many free stamens from the separate pistils/carpels; in Aquilegia trace those carpels into several dry FOLLICLES that open lengthwise. This anatomy is not proven by the two existing general columbine photos.
steps.why_it_matters: A flower center plus its mature fruit provides stronger family evidence than color, spurs or a vine habit alone.

comparisons.title: Ranunculaceae vs Rosaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have many stamens and free carpels. Rosaceae commonly has stipules plus a hypanthium; Ranunculaceae usually lacks both.

comparisons.title: Ranunculaceae vs Papaveraceae
comparisons.rule: Poppies commonly have caducous sepals, free petals and a syncarpous capsule; Ranunculaceae commonly keeps free carpels or aggregate fruits.

comparisons.title: Clematis vs Aquilegia — both Ranunculaceae
comparisons.rule: Clematis has four showy sepals with no true petals and usually achene fruit. Aquilegia has five showy sepals plus FIVE SPURRED true petals and fruits of follicles; see the real photos before memorizing terminology.

visual_lesson.caveat: Ranunculaceae is diverse: Clematis's opposite leaves and missing true petals are not family-wide rules. Only use a precise arrow for a petal spur, achene body, petal/sepal boundary, or free carpel after the structure is actually visible and its coordinates have been verified. All images in this lesson are already physically installed; they do not prove every diagnostic microstructure.

family_confusion_cleanup.field_question: What exact floral or fruit structure confirms this family, and which nearby family could mimic it?
look_here_first: Inspect flower center for numerous free stamens and mostly free carpels, typically with superior ovaries.
Identify showy sepals vs true petals before counting petals.
Look for achene aggregates or follicles and check for absence of a typical Rosaceae hypanthium.

comparison_matrix.separate: Both may have many stamens and free carpels; Rosaceae commonly has a hypanthium and stipules, unlike most Ranunculaceae.
Argemone has caducous sepals and a syncarpous capsule, unlike Clematis aggregate achenes and free carpels; compare fruit and gynoecium.
Clematis has showy petaloid sepals but no true petals and achene fruits; Aquilegia has petal spurs and follicle fruits.

genus_routing_cues: Clematis: opposite divided leaves, petaloid sepals, numerous free stamens/carpels and plumose or persistent achene styles.
Aquilegia: five petal spurs, showy sepals and follicle cluster; only use canonical species imagery where available.
Ranunculus: separate free petals and achenes; distinguish from Clematis without requiring petaloid sepals.
